issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court is not compelled to refer an omitted material issue to the trial court under the procedure for additional findings, and remand should not be ordered routinely.
material_facts: A decree was appealed, and the written statement was amended during the appeal, after which additional factual and legal issues were framed.
The first appellate court remanded the matter to the trial court, reasoning that it should not itself record evidence and decide the new issues.
The High Court set aside that remand and directed the first appellate court to decide the appeal on its merits, while noting that referral could be considered if evidence was insufficient.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to set aside the remand and require the first appellate court to decide the appeal on its merits; referral of an essential omitted issue is discretionary, not compulsory, and remand is not routine.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies when the lower court omitted to frame or try an issue, or determine a material question of fact, that the appellate court considers essential to the decision on the merits. The appellate court may refer the issue if necessary, but is not compelled to do so merely because an issue was omitted. The first appellate court is the final court on facts and may decide the issue itself. The Court relied on Gogula Gurumurthy v. Kurimeti Ayyappa for the proposition that receiving findings on referred issues does not dispose of the appeal and the parties remain entitled to argue the whole appeal afterward.

predicates.first_appeal_from_original_decree: A party has brought a first appeal from a decree made in an original proceeding.
predicates.lower_court_omitted_essential_issue: The court whose decree is appealed omitted to frame or try an issue, or determine a factual question, that the appellate court considers essential to deciding the merits.

issues.definition: When an essential issue was omitted in a first appeal from an original decree, the appellate court may choose whether to refer that issue for findings.

issues.legal_issue: When an appellate court refers an omitted issue for trial and additional evidence is required, the trial court must take that evidence and return it with findings and reasons.
material_facts: The dispute was before a first appellate court after amendment of the written statement and the framing of additional issues.
The procedure at issue provides for the appellate court to refer an essential omitted issue and direct the lower court to take any additional evidence required.
The Supreme Court distinguished the appellate court’s discretion to refer an issue from the lower court’s obligation to take and return required evidence once such a direction is made.
issues.conclusion: If the appellate court directs the lower court to try a referred issue and additional evidence is required, the lower court must take that evidence and return it with its findings and reasons.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes referral discretionary for the appellate court, but provides that the lower court shall try the referred issue and return the evidence, findings, and reasons. The obligation to take additional evidence applies where such evidence is required. Under Gogula Gurumurthy v. Kurimeti Ayyappa, receipt of findings on referred issues does not dispose of the appeal, and the parties may argue the whole appeal afterward.

predicates.first_appeal_from_original_decree: A party has brought a first appeal from a decree made in an original proceeding.
predicates.appellate_court_referred_issue: The appellate court has referred an issue to the court whose decree is under appeal for trial and findings.
predicates.additional_evidence_required: Evidence beyond that already available is needed to try the referred issue.

issues.definition: If a first appellate court refers an issue and additional evidence is needed, the lower court must take and return that evidence along with findings and reasons.

issues.legal_issue: Whether statutory language is mandatory or directory depends on legislative intent and context, not on the words “may” or “shall” alone.
material_facts: The procedure under consideration used “may” for the appellate court’s decision to refer issues and “shall” for the lower court’s tasks after referral.
The dispute required determining whether the use of “may” made referral obligatory despite its permissive wording.
The Court considered the provision’s scheme and purpose, the role of the first appellate court, and the consequences of treating referral as mandatory or discretionary.
issues.conclusion: The words “may” and “shall” are not conclusive; the court must determine legislative intent from the provision’s purpose, scheme, context, and the consequences of the competing constructions.
issues.legal_principle: The mandatory or directory character of a statutory provision is determined by legislative intent rather than by the word used in isolation. Relevant considerations include the statute’s scheme, purpose and object, the context and background of the language, the consequences or inconvenience of each construction, and whether public convenience or the statutory objective would be defeated. The Court relied on Julius v. Lord Bishop of Oxford, Padfield v. Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries & Food, Commissioner of Police v. Gordhandas Bhanji, Ratlam Municipality v. Vardichan, and M/s. Dhampur Sugar Mills Ltd. v. State of U.P., among other authorities.

predicates.statutory_provision_interpretation_case: A court must determine the legal effect of language in a statutory provision.
predicates.provision_uses_may_or_shall: The provision uses words such as “may” or “shall” in describing a power or duty.
predicates.purpose_scheme_context_and_consequences_: The provision’s purpose, scheme, context, and consequences of alternative readings bear on its intended effect.

issues.definition: When a statutory provision uses “may” or “shall,” its effect is determined from legislative intent assessed in context rather than from that word alone.
